questions.question: When should Go code return an error instead of panicking?
questions.title: Errors for expected failure, panic for broken invariants
questions.direct_answer: Return an error for failures a caller can reasonably encounter or respond to, including invalid input, missing files, timeouts, and unavailable dependencies. Reserve panic for broken internal invariants, programmer mistakes, or initialization states where continuing is impossible; library APIs should normally keep panics from crossing their boundary.

interviewer_intent.testing: The recoverability boundary between ordinary failures and violated invariants.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using panic as a shortcut for every error or recovering so broadly that serious bugs disappear.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Classify the same event differently based on whether external input or an internal invariant caused it.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Return errors for expected operational and input failures.
Use panic for impossible states or programmer errors, not ordinary branching.
A panic unwinds the current goroutine and runs deferred calls.
Public library functions should normally report failures as errors.
Initialization may panic when the program genuinely cannot start.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I return an error when failure is part of normal operation and the caller can choose a response. Bad input, a missing record, permission denial, network timeout, and full disk are all ordinary possibilities even when they are inconvenient. An error keeps that choice explicit in the function's contract.

I reserve panic for conditions that indicate the program's assumptions are broken, such as an unreachable internal state, an out-of-range access, or mandatory initialization that makes startup meaningless. Panic begins unwinding the current goroutine and runs deferred functions, so it is much more disruptive than an ordinary return.

For example, parsing a user-supplied date should return an error because the user can correct it. If an internal enum reaches a branch proven impossible after validation, a panic may expose a programming defect rather than disguising it as routine bad input. The cause and recovery options determine the form, not how annoying the failure is.

Library APIs should normally avoid letting explicit panics escape; callers cannot handle them with normal control flow. A package may use panic internally to simplify deeply nested work, but its exported boundary should convert expected internal panics to an error and re-panic unexpected runtime faults. I choose error by default and require a strong invariant-based reason for panic.

sections.title: Classify by who can recover
sections.content:
External systems and users routinely produce unsuccessful outcomes. These belong in values because callers may retry, translate, report, or ignore them according to policy. A broken invariant indicates that the code's own model is no longer trustworthy.

Panic is therefore not an error severity level. A temporary network outage may be severe but recoverable; a tiny impossible state may reveal a bug and deserve a crash. The useful distinction is whether ordinary callers are expected to continue.

sections.title: Choose by failure meaning
sections.content:
| Situation | Preferred signal | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Invalid user input | return `error` | Caller can request correction |
| Missing file | return `error` | Caller may choose another path |
| Network timeout | return `error` | Retry or fallback may be valid |
| Broken internal invariant | `panic` may be appropriate | Continuing can hide a programming defect |
| Required startup configuration absent | error to main or panic at startup boundary | Process cannot serve correctly |

questions.question: How do defer and recover work during a panic?
questions.title: Panic unwinding and recover
questions.direct_answer: A panic stops normal execution in the current function and unwinds that goroutine's stack, running deferred calls in each frame. `recover` can stop the panic only when called directly by a deferred function on that same goroutine; the recovering function then returns to its caller rather than resuming at the panic site.

interviewer_intent.testing: Exact stack-unwinding, defer, same-goroutine, and resume semantics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling recover in an ordinary function or expecting execution to resume after panic.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace control from the panic site through deferred cleanup to the caller of the recovery boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Panic stops the current function's normal instruction flow.
Deferred calls run while stack frames unwind.
Recover is effective only when called directly by a deferred function.
Recovery works only in the panicking goroutine.
Execution does not continue at the statement after panic.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
When `panic` runs, the current function stops ordinary execution. Go begins unwinding the current goroutine's call stack, and each active function runs its deferred calls in last-in, first-out order before its frame is discarded. If nothing recovers, unwinding reaches the goroutine's top and the program reports the panic.

`recover` can stop that sequence only when it is called directly by a deferred function in the same goroutine. In that situation it returns the value passed to `panic`. Calling recover during normal execution returns nil, and a defer in another goroutine cannot catch this panic.

For example, `safeDivide` can defer a closure that calls recover, invoke code that panics on a zero divisor, and convert the recovered value into an error. The divide function does not continue after the panic statement. Instead, the recovery boundary finishes its deferred work and returns to its caller.

Recovery should sit at a clear boundary and preserve evidence, often including a stack trace. It is not a substitute for returning errors from expected failures. Broad recovery that silently continues can leave state uncertain and hide defects. I use it to contain a request, worker, or package-internal panic, then translate known cases or re-panic unexpected ones.

sections.title: Unwind one stack frame at a time
sections.content:
A deferred cleanup still runs because it was registered before normal execution stopped. This lets files close, locks release, and boundary code observe the panic. Each caller frame follows the same rule until recovery or termination.

Recovery ends unwinding, but it does not rewind program state or retry the failed instruction. Functions between the boundary and panic site have already been abandoned. The boundary must return a well-defined result rather than pretending nothing happened.

sections.title: Control flow during recovery
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Caller
  participant S as safeDivide
  participant D as divide
  C->>S: call
  S->>S: register deferred recovery
  S->>D: divide by zero
  D-->>S: panic unwinds
  S->>S: deferred function calls recover
  S-->>C: return converted error
```

questions.question: Where should recover be placed in a Go server or worker?
questions.title: Recovery at request and worker boundaries
questions.direct_answer: Place recovery around an independent unit of work—such as an HTTP request handler or one worker job—so one unexpected panic can be recorded and contained without hiding failures elsewhere. The deferred recovery must run in the same goroutine, establish a safe result, and re-panic values it is not designed to handle.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical containment, goroutine ownership, observability, and safe post-panic state.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting one recover around a goroutine launcher and assuming it protects child goroutines.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a wrapper that contains one job while keeping later jobs available.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Recover around one independent request, task, or package boundary.
Install the deferred recovery inside the goroutine doing the work.
Record the panic value and stack before translating it.
Return a safe failure result; do not continue corrupted work.
Re-panic unexpected categories when the boundary cannot guarantee safety.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I place recover at a boundary that owns one isolated unit of work, such as one HTTP request, queue message, plugin call, or worker job. That boundary can convert an unexpected panic into a failed request or task while allowing unrelated work to continue. Recovery deep inside ordinary helpers makes control flow difficult to reason about.

The deferred function must be installed in the same goroutine that might panic. A recover in the parent that launched `go work()` cannot catch a panic inside `work`; each goroutine has its own stack. The worker entry function therefore wraps the job before calling application logic.

For example, a job runner can defer a closure, call `recover`, record the panic and stack, set the job result to failed, and return. The loop then accepts the next job. It must not resume the interrupted job because intermediate state may be incomplete.

A recovery boundary should distinguish panics it knows how to translate from unexpected runtime defects. Package-internal code may recover only its own private panic type and re-panic anything else. Server middleware may contain all request panics for availability, but still records enough detail for diagnosis. The purpose is controlled isolation, not making defects invisible.

sections.title: Match the recovery scope to the failure scope
sections.content:
Independent work units already have a natural success-or-failure boundary. Installing recovery there gives the system a valid next action: finish this request with an error, mark this job failed, or reject this plugin result. The rest of the process remains outside the damaged call stack.

The wrapper also centralizes observability. It can attach request or job identity, capture the stack, and emit one failure record. Lower helpers stay honest by using ordinary errors for expected outcomes.

sections.title: Contain one job without hiding the panic
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Worker receives job] --> B[Install deferred recovery]
  B --> C[Run job in same goroutine]
  C --> D{Outcome}
  D -- success --> E[Mark complete]
  D -- returned error --> F[Mark failed]
  D -- panic --> G[Recover, record stack, mark failed]
  E --> H[Receive next job]
  F --> H
  G --> H
```
